clue.text: Yearn for the chap who wrote Ultima The

parts.note: to yearn is to long
a chap is a fellow

explanation.surface: Someone pines for the man who wrote a book of poems.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as printed ends 'Ultima The', an OCR slip for Ultima Thule, an 1880 collection of poems by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow; 'for' only links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The American poet published the collection Ultima Thule late in his life.

clue.text: Part of actor on telly, a friend of Alceste

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A television performer plays a role in Molière's comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Molière's The Misanthrope, Oronte is the sonnet-writing courtier who seeks Alceste's friendship.
explanation.definitionFit: In Molière's play the courtier Oronte offers himself as a companion to the misanthrope Alceste.

clue.text: Choke about wall being smashed — what a pest!

indicators.note: about means the gasping word goes around the other piece

parts.note: to choke is to gasp for breath

indicators.note: being smashed means the letters of wall are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone splutters on seeing a wall knocked down by a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts ALLW, the anagram of WALL from 'being smashed', inside GASP.
explanation.definitionFit: A gall wasp is an insect that damages plants by making galls, so gardeners count it a pest.

clue.text: Consummate outcome? You crew, so they say

parts.note: an outcome is an effect

indicators.note: so they say signals that the words are heard spoken, not spelt

parts.note: you sounds like the letter U, and a rowing crew is an eight

explanation.surface: A question about the result of crowning a deal, addressed to a boat's team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so they say' makes U EIGHT into the spelling UATE: 'you' is said like U and 'eight', a rowing crew, like ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To consummate something is to bring it to completion, which is to accomplish or effect it.

clue.text: Allergy suffered in very big way

indicators.note: suffered suggests the letters have been put through an ordeal and come out rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone's hay fever struck them badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Largely means to a great extent, that is, on a big scale.

clue.text: Bird starting to roost in Cobbett's great city

indicators.note: in places the first letter of roost inside the city's name

parts.note: William Cobbett called London 'the Great Wen', a wen being a swelling

indicators.note: starting to picks the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A bird begins to settle for the night in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: William Cobbett, the 19th-century English writer, called London 'the Great Wen', a wen being a swelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The wren is a tiny brown songbird.

clue.text: Ruler of London is tops — good and witty

indicators.note: tops says to take the top, that is the first letter, of each of the preceding words

parts.note: arch means playfully sly or witty

explanation.surface: A wealthy power-broker in London is praised as excellent company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tops' takes the first letters of 'of London is', giving OLI.
explanation.definitionFit: An oligarch is one of a small group holding power, a ruler in a narrow regime.

clue.text: Stymies our broadcast of Christie's Affair?

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: A radio version of an Agatha Christie novel is blocked.
explanation.walkthrough: Agatha Christie's first novel was The Mysterious Affair at Styles; 'of' links.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective in the title of Christie's debut novel describes the puzzling affair at Styles.

clue.text: Have trust about one that's liberal, truly

indicators.note: about means the trusting word goes around the other pieces

parts.note: to have trust in is to rely
one is the indefinite article a

explanation.surface: Someone is told to trust a liberal-minded person honestly.
explanation.definitionFit: Really and truly are both adverbs meaning genuinely or in fact.

clue.text: Cartoonist — career right for criminal, say?

parts.note: David Low was a famous political cartoonist
a career is one's working life

explanation.surface: A cartoonist changes career for the right reasons.
explanation.walkthrough: David Low was a New Zealand-born cartoonist on London's Evening Standard, famous for Colonel Blimp.
explanation.definitionFit: A lowlifer is a disreputable person, of which a crook is one example.

clue.text: Where this battle occurred is described as OK!

definitions.text: Where this battle occurred is described as OK!

parts.words: Where this battle occurred is described as OK!
parts.note: the famous Wild West shoot-out took place at the O.K. Corral in Tombstone, Arizona

explanation.surface: A battlefield is declared to be all right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'OK' looks like approval, but it names the O.K. Corral, where the Earps fought the Clantons in 1881.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1881 shoot-out at the O.K. Corral was an exchange of pistol fire.

clue.text: You'll have to have one of this Japanese shoe

parts.words: You'll have to have one of this Japanese shoe
parts.note: the clue's instruction to acquire one of the shoes, put in two everyday words, also spells out the shoe's own name

explanation.surface: A shop assistant insists you buy this Japanese footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says you must 'get a' one, and those two words run together give the name of the wooden clog.
explanation.definitionFit: The geta is a raised wooden sandal traditionally worn in Japan.

clue.text: Global hope ruined, hating such as Voltaire

definitions.note: the definition is a phrase describing a person who hates the French, Voltaire being one

indicators.note: ruined means the letters of the phrase are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Hopes for the world are dashed by someone hating a French philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: Voltaire is the example of a Frenchman: the answer is someone hostile to the French.
explanation.definitionFit: A Gallophobe dislikes France and its people, Voltaire being a typical Frenchman.

clue.text: Mole or Rat relate about carrying Pooh

indicators.note: carrying means the rearranged letters hold the bear inside them
about here means turned around, so the letters of relate are rearranged

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh is a bear

explanation.surface: Characters from children's stories tell a tale involving A. A. Milne's bear.
explanation.walkthrough: Mole and Rat look like Kenneth Grahame's animals from The Wind in the Willows, but each is slang for an informer; 'carrying' puts BEAR inside TALEER, the anagram of RELATE from 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mole or a rat betrays secrets, and a talebearer is a telltale who passes them on.

clue.text: Style of guitar, needing courage and cheek

parts.note: bottle is British slang for courage
neck is British slang for cheek or impudence

explanation.surface: A guitarist needs nerve and some brass to play.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'bottle' is courage and 'neck' is cheek; 'needing' and 'and' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottleneck is a slide style of blues guitar, played with a glass neck on the finger.

clue.text: A quiet delay comes round every fourth year!

indicators.note: comes round means the letters turn about into a new arrangement

parts.note: P, from piano, is the musical abbreviation for quiet

explanation.surface: A gentle postponement recurs once in four years.
explanation.definitionFit: February 29th is added in years divisible by four, as a leap year's extra day.

clue.text: Hohenheim's spirit, "originally" Greek!

parts.note: Paracelsus, born Theophrastus von Hohenheim, named a vital spirit from a Greek word meaning original or ancient

explanation.surface: An alchemist's guiding spirit turns out to be Greek at root.
explanation.walkthrough: Hohenheim is Paracelsus, the Swiss physician, whose life-force took its name from Greek arkhaios, 'original'.
explanation.definitionFit: Paracelsus coined the term for the vital force governing life, borrowing a Greek word for first or original.

clue.text: Sneeze that demands just one hanky, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the words are heard spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a single paper handkerchief is a tissue

explanation.surface: A sneeze calls for only a single handkerchief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns 'a tissue', said aloud, into the sound of a sneeze; 'that demands' links.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the conventional spelling of the noise made when sneezing.

clue.text: Endure his seduction in poem by

parts.note: to endure is to stand something

indicators.note: seduction means the letters of his are led astray into a new order

explanation.surface: A suitor endures his wooing in a Longfellow poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem by Longfellow (1-across) is The Courtship of Miles Standish.
explanation.definitionFit: Miles Standish is the Plymouth captain in Longfellow's narrative poem of courtship.

clue.text: Case to connect with conclusion of Donne

parts.note: to connect

indicators.note: conclusion of picks the last letter of the poet's name

explanation.surface: A connection is made with the end of a poem by John Donne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is not a legal case but an attaché case, a slim briefcase; 'to' and 'with' link.
explanation.definitionFit: An attaché case is a slim briefcase, so the word alone serves for the bag.

clue.text: Commander and hero, drunk, leant to the West

parts.note: OC is the military abbreviation for officer commanding
El Cid is the Spanish national hero

indicators.note: drunk means the letters of leant stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: An officer and a hero, both drunk, leaned westward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges LEANT to ENTAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Occidental means western, from the Latin for the setting sun.

clue.text: From swank, Royal Society's after the best

indicators.note: after places the society's letters behind the best

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, the best, with the numeral read as I
RS is the abbreviation for the Royal Society

explanation.surface: From showing off, a learned society comes after the finest.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means first-class; its 1 is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Swank is pretentious showing off, which is putting on affected manners.

clue.text: Heartless ride about night-time, resistance his ride?

indicators.note: about means the shortened word goes around the other pieces
heartless means the middle letters of ride are removed

parts.note: eve is the evening
R is the physics abbreviation for resistance

explanation.surface: A rider sets out at night against opposition on a famous mission.
explanation.walkthrough: The page shows 'ruse' where Paul Revere's 'ride' is meant. 'Heartless' turns RIDE into RE, which goes 'about' EVE and R; Revere's midnight ride of 1775 is celebrated by Longfellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow's poem 'Paul Revere's Ride' tells of the patriot's midnight gallop.

clue.text: Ah! What I translated? A poem by

indicators.note: translated means the letters are turned into a new order

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a translation of a Longfellow poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem by Longfellow (1-across) is The Song of Hiawatha.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiawatha is the hero of Longfellow's long narrative poem set among the Ojibwe.

clue.text: Thanks to heartlands of Russia, it brought all the news

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks

indicators.note: heartlands of picks the middle letters of the country's name

explanation.surface: Gratitude to the Russian interior for bringing all the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ta' is British informal for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: TASS was the Soviet news agency, the official source of news in the USSR.

clue.text: … a poem composed while E.C. takes a run?

indicators.note: composed means the letters are put together in a new order

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A poem is written while E. C. Bentley goes jogging.
explanation.walkthrough: E. C. Bentley invented the comic four-line verse that bears his middle name; 'takes' adds R to the anagram pool and 'a' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerihew is a short comic verse about a famous person, invented by Edmund Clerihew Bentley.

clue.text: Be about to have sex, a bit sultry, the pigs!

indicators.note: about means the letters of be go around the other piece

parts.note: taken as written
to rut is to mate, as deer do

indicators.note: a bit picks just a small piece, the first letter, of the next word

explanation.surface: An outburst at boorish men getting amorous in the heat.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutes and pigs are both insults for coarse, beastly people.

clue.text: If the snake is resolved, he'll burgle your digs

indicators.note: is resolved means the letters are worked out into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Once the snake problem is solved, a burglar will rob your lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digs' is British slang for lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: A sneak thief steals from homes without force, slipping in unnoticed.
